description: CiteVerify reasoning benchmark: claims with fixed evidence passages (from evidence-snapshot.json). All labels are provisional until a human reviewer validates them; altered cases are synthetic by design. Since 2026-11-20 the app reports irrelevant (possibly mis-cited) evidence as Unable to verify with a note, not as Unsupported.

cases.claim: Menopause is associated with atherogenic changes, including a worsening of cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk factors1–3 and decreased aerobic fitness4 compared with premenopausal women.
cases.rationale: Reference 4 shows lower VO2max and worse LDL/glucose in post- versus perimenopausal women (compared with peri-, not pre-menopausal women). References 1 and 3 are about FMD as a diagnostic or prognostic test and do not address menopause; reference 2 likewise concerns FMD prognosis.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Similarly, vascular endothelial function measured via flow-mediated dilation (FMD) is impaired after menopause.56
cases.rationale: Reference 6 reports lower FMD in postmenopausal than premenopausal women; reference 5 reports endothelium-dependent vasodilation impaired after menopause (measured by plethysmography, not FMD).
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: This initially may be due to a decrease in endogenous oestrogen levels,7 and likely further exacerbated by increased adiposity8 and reductions in exercise habits or physical activity levels.8
cases.rationale: Reference 8 supports increased adiposity and reduced leisure-time physical activity at menopause. Reference 7's abstract concerns acute exercise effects and says nothing about oestrogen as a cause.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Because endothelial dysfunction may represent one of the early subclinical events in atherogenesis,9 and has been shown to predict future risk of hypertension10 and cardiovascular events11 in postmenopausal women, effective intervention strategies capable of improving endothelial function are needed.
cases.rationale: References 10 and 11 support FMD predicting hypertension and cardiovascular events in postmenopausal women. Reference 9's abstract (leukocyte adhesion molecules) does not state that endothelial dysfunction is an early event in atherogenesis.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Aerobic exercise training as an intervention has been shown to improve endothelial function consistently in individuals with CVD risk12–15 and hypertension.141617
cases.rationale: References 13-17 report improved endothelial function with training in groups with CVD risk (review, metabolic syndrome, post-MI) and hypertension.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Aerobic exercise is believed to improve endothelial function by increasing antegrade vascular shear stress, which leads to upregulation of nitric oxide synthase, and greater nitric oxide release.13
cases.rationale: Reference 13 describes shear-stress stimulation of NO bioactivity and up-regulated eNOS with exercise training.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: The results of the present study suggest that moderate intensity aerobic exercise training may have cardioprotective benefits because improvements in endothelial function are associated with reduced risk of cardiovascular events in postmenopausal women.11
cases.rationale: Reference 11 shows lower FMD predicts cardiovascular events in postmenopausal women, but not that improving FMD reduces risk; the cardioprotection inference is the authors'.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: There are three published studies to our knowledge which have found no improvement in endothelial function in healthy postmenopausal women after aerobic exercise training.27–29
cases.rationale: Reference 29 found no FMD change in post-menopausal women after aerobic training, and reference 27 no FMD change after training. Reference 28's abstract reports that training improved NO dilator function (FMD-to-GTN ratio) in older sedentary women, which cuts against the claim.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Casey et al27 found no significant change in FMD after 18 weeks of treadmill training in healthy subjects (n=10).
cases.rationale: Reference 27 (PubMed record) randomised women to 18 weeks of resistance or aerobic training (aerobic n=10); brachial FMD did not change significantly in either group.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Recently, Pierce et al29 found no improvement in FMD in postmenopausal women with no CVD, but they found improvement in older men.
cases.rationale: Reference 29: brachial FMD increased >50% in middle-aged/older men but did not change in post-menopausal women without CVD.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Our results are in line with previous studies, because differences in improvements in endothelial function after exercise training are likely explained by the fact that our subjects had elevated blood pressure (which is associated with endothelial dysfunction),30 and presented with lower FMD values at baseline (4.1%) than the previous training studies in postmenopausal women already mentioned (Casey et al: 9.9%, Black et al: 5.3%, Pierce et al: 5.1%).27–29
cases.rationale: Reference 30 links hypertension with endothelial dysfunction and reference 29's women had baseline FMD 5.1%, as stated. Reference 28's abstract gives 4.3% for older sedentary women, not 5.3%; Casey's 9.9% is not in reference 27's abstract.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: In addition, subject populations with elevated blood pressure have shown improvement in FMD with aerobic exercise training. 141617
cases.rationale: References 16 and 17 report improved FMD with training in hypertensive patients; reference 14 in metabolic syndrome.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Tinken et al31 observed evidence of vascular remodelling during cycle ergometer exercise training in young healthy subjects because FMD increased after 2 and 4 weeks but was not significantly different from baseline at 6 or 8 weeks.
cases.rationale: Reference 31: brachial FMD rose at weeks 2 and 4 and returned toward baseline by week 8 while dilator capacity rose (remodelling). Week 6 is not stated for the brachial artery in the abstract.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Approximately, 70% of exercisers in the present study presented with endothelial dysfunction, which was expected because our participants had elevated blood pressure30 and were post-menopausal.5
cases.rationale: The cited associations hold: reference 30 (hypertension and endothelial dysfunction) and reference 5 (menopause and endothelial dysfunction). The 70% figure is the paper's own result.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: This may explain why there is generally a consistent improvement in endothelial function in individuals with CVD risk, and inconsistent results in apparently healthy subjects in response to exercise training.13
cases.rationale: Reference 13: improvement is consistent in subjects with CVD and risk factors and less frequently found in healthy subjects.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: In addition, FMD normalisation via shear AUC may violate several statistical assumptions33 and may even introduce errors into the measurement.32
cases.rationale: Reference 32 recommends not normalising FMD for shear (relationship is age dependent). Reference 33's abstract is a methods tutorial and does not state the statistical-assumption point.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Lastly, previous studies have observed significant relationships between FMD uncorrected for shear and CVD risk.113435
cases.rationale: Reference 11 (FMD predicts cardiovascular events) and reference 34 (FMD related to CVD risk factors in the community) support the relationship; reference 35's abstract was not reviewed.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Refutation and controversy is seen across the range of research designs, from clinical trials and traditional epidemiological studies [1–3] to the most modern molecular research [4,5].
cases.rationale: Refs 4-5 show unstable molecular signatures and frequent between-study heterogeneity in genetics (molecular part); refs 1-3 on trials and epidemiology have no accessible text.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: There is increasing concern that in modern research, false findings may be the majority or even the vast majority of published research claims [6–8].
cases.rationale: Ref 6 reports increasing scepticism from failures to replicate; no passage says false findings are the majority, and ref 7 says a sizeable proportion of associations are probably true.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: Modeling the Framework for False Positive Findings Several methodologists have pointed out [9–11] that the high rate of nonreplication (lack of confi rmation) of research discoveries is a consequence of the convenient, yet ill-founded strategy of claiming conclusive research findings solely on the basis of a single study assessed by formal statistical significance, typically for a p-value less than 0.05.
cases.rationale: Ref 10 says too many reported associations are false positives, largely because significance is declared from a P value alone below .05; ref 9 has no accessible text.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: As has been shown previously, the probability that a research finding is indeed true depends on the prior probability of it being true (before doing the study), the statistical power of the study, and the level of statistical significance [10,11].
cases.rationale: Ref 10: the false positive report probability depends on the P value and on the prior probability and statistical power.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: The PPV is also the complementary probability of what Wacholder et al. have called the false positive report probability [10].
cases.rationale: Ref 10 (Wacholder et al.) defines the false positive report probability; that PPV is its complement is the author's definitional step.
cases.labelledBy: AI-assisted (Claude Opus 5.5), judged only against the evidence passages listed

cases.claim: For example, with large measurement errors relationships are lost in noise [12], or investigators use data inefficiently or fail to notice statistically significant relationships, or there may be conflicts of interest that tend to “bury” significant findings [13].

cases.claim: Thus, other factors being equal, research findings are more likely true in scientific fields that undertake large studies, such as randomized controlled trials in cardiology (several thousand subjects randomized) [14] than in scientific fields with small studies, such as most research of molecular predictors (sample sizes 100-fold smaller) [15].
cases.rationale: Ref 14 is metadata only; ref 15's abstract concerns validating prognostic models and says nothing about study sizes or how often findings are true.

cases.claim: Thus research findings are more likely true in scientific fields with large effects, such as the impact of smoking on cancer or cardiovascular disease (relative risks 3–20), than in scientific fi elds where postulated effects are small, such as genetic risk factors for multigenetic diseases (relative risks 1.1–1.5) [7].
